blocks.title: What the interviewer is really testing
blocks.text: This is not a chess-rules quiz. It is a **polymorphism and ownership** test. Anyone can write an 8x8 array and a giant `switch` on piece type. The interviewer wants to see where you put **move geometry vs move legality vs game state**, and whether that split survives the three killers: **leaving your own king in check, special moves, and checkmate detection**. Put geometry in pieces, legality in the game, state in the board — and say why every other split rots.
The problem

Design a playable two-player chess game with full move validation. Support the standard 8x8 board, all six piece types with their legal moves, captures, turn alternation, and detection of **check, checkmate, and stalemate**. Support the four special rules that separate a toy from a correct solution: **castling, en passant, pawn promotion, and pawn double-step**. The design must be extensible — adding a new variant or an undo feature must not require rewriting the move validator — and the core `makeMove` path must be obviously correct under time pressure.

items: `Game.makeMove(Player p, int fromRow, int fromCol, int toRow, int toCol)` — validates turn, piece ownership, piece geometry, path blocking, and king safety; executes capture / promotion / castling / en passant; then updates game status. Returns `true` on success, `false` with reason on illegal move.

`Piece.canMove(Board b, Spot from, Spot to)` — pure geometry plus blocking, **no** knowledge of check or turn. Each subclass (`King`, `Queen`, `Rook`, `Bishop`, `Knight`, `Pawn`) owns only its own shape.
`Game.getStatus()` — returns `IN_PROGRESS`, `WHITE_WINS`, `BLACK_WINS`, `STALEMATE`, or `DRAW`. Computed after every move, never cached inside pieces.

blocks.text: Clarify before you code

Do not start with classes. Start with scope, because chess has an infinite tail of rules and the interviewer is watching what you bound. Five sharp questions buy you the whole design. State your assumptions out loud — most candidates silently pick the wrong ones and pay for it during castling.

items.title: Human vs human, or engine?
items.text: Agree you are building a local 2-player rules engine, not search, not AI, not networking. No minimax, no clock unless asked. This keeps the problem in OOP instead of algorithms.

items.title: Which rules are in scope?
items.text: Confirm check and checkmate are required, then force a decision on the big four: castling, en passant, promotion, pawn double-step. Say you will implement all four but triage checkmate first — that ordering is what strong candidates do.

items.title: How are moves input?
items.text: Coordinates (`e2-e4`) or `Spot` objects? Agree board is 0-7 indexed, white starts at rows 6-7 moving up. This kills half the off-by-one bugs before they happen.

items.title: Undo, timers, draw rules?
items.text: Ask if `undo`, move history, 50-move rule, threefold repetition, or timed play are needed. Default answer: keep a `List<Move>` history so undo and repetition are cheap later, but do not build clocks now.

items.title: Illegal move contract?
items.text: Exception or boolean? Agree on `boolean` plus `GameStatus` for the skeleton, exceptions for programming errors. This avoids a 5-minute argument mid-coding.

blocks.text: Requirements agreed

blocks.caption: Scope to lock before writing code.
rows: Defines initial state; no custom variants
Pawn promotion (default to queen, allow choice)
This is where naive designs collapse
Move validation O(1) to O(7) steps
Board is fixed size; clarity beats micro-optimisation
Extensible: new piece or rule without editing Game

blocks.text: Approach 1 — the flat switch

The tempting start is one `Board` class with `int[8][8]` and a single `isValidMove(from, to)` containing a `switch(pieceType)` with seven branches, each with its own loop for sliding pieces. Pawn logic sprawls across 40 lines. Castling becomes an `if` tucked inside the king branch. Check detection becomes a second giant loop that duplicates the first. It passes the happy path in ten minutes, which is exactly why weak candidates pick it.

This fails for three structural reasons, not stylistic ones. First, it violates **single responsibility**: one method knows rook sliding, pawn double-step, and castling rights — any rule change touches the same 200 lines. **Trade-off:** you gain speed of writing, you lose every follow-up. Second, check detection cannot reuse anything, so candidates copy-paste move logic into `isInCheck()` and the two copies drift. Third, special moves need cross-move state — `hasMoved` for castling, `last double-step pawn` for en passant — and there is nowhere to store it except globals or extra parameters threaded through the switch. The moment the interviewer says *now add checkmate*, this design requires a rewrite. Name that explicitly in the interview, then discard it.
The real design — pieces own geometry, game owns legality

Split into three layers with hard boundaries. **Piece** answers one question: *ignoring check, could I geometrically move from A to B on this board?* That includes blocking for sliders but nothing else. **Board** answers: *what is where, and is the path clear?* It owns the grid and piece lookup, nothing about turns. **Game** answers: *is this move legal right now?* It checks turn, ownership, destination occupancy, executes the move on a trial basis, then rejects anything that leaves the mover's own king in check. **Why this split?** Geometry changes per piece but never needs game state; legality needs game state but never needs geometry details. Each layer can be tested alone. The cost is one extra indirection per move — irrelevant on an 8x8 board — and the payoff is that checkmate becomes a loop over existing primitives instead of new logic.

blocks.title: Move validation pipeline
blocks.caption: Every makeMove flows through the same five gates in order.
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  A[Caller calls Game makeMove] --> B[Turn and ownership check]
  B --> C[Piece canMove geometry]
  C --> D[Special moves castling enpassant promotion]
  D --> E[Trial move then own-king-in-check test]
  E --> F[Commit and update status]

blocks.text: Board representation is a deliberate boring choice: `Spot[8][8]` where each `Spot` holds a `Piece` or null, plus `whiteToMove`, `lastMove`, and castling flags. Alternatives sound clever and hurt you. Bitboards are 10x faster for engines but unreadable in an interview and hostile to `canMove` polymorphism — **trade-off:** raw speed versus clarity and extensibility, and the interview grades the second. A `Map<Position, Piece>` saves memory on sparse boards, but chess is dense and indexed access `board[r][c]` is O(1) and obvious. Keep the grid. Store `hasMoved` on each piece for castling and pawn double-step, and store `lastMove` on the game for en passant. Do not store attacked-square caches yet — recompute on demand; the board is tiny and caching introduces invalidation bugs you cannot afford in 45 minutes.

blocks.title: Core class structure
blocks.caption: Piece hierarchy isolates movement; Game orchestrates turns and king safety.

blocks.text: Working code — Java core

Read the Java in layers. `Board.isSquareAttacked` deliberately special-cases pawns: a pawn's `canMove` requires an enemy on the target square, but attack means *could capture if an enemy were there*. Without that branch, kings could walk next to pawns and check detection would silently miss. That is the single most common latent bug in interview code — the tests pass until someone writes a pawn-check case. Similarly, castling and en passant live in `Game`, not in `King` or `Pawn`, because they need `lastMove` and attacked-square queries that pieces must never see. **Trade-off:** `Game` grows longer, but pieces stay pure and unit-testable without a game harness.
Complexity

blocks.caption: Costs on a fixed 8x8 board — state them to show you measured.
rows: Scans all pieces; fine at this size
~4k trial moves worst case; trivial for humans, too slow for engines
Board plus move list for undo/repetition

blocks.text: The hardest follow-up — check, mate, and stalemate

Everything funnels into one primitive: *is square X attacked by side Y?* Check is that primitive applied to the king's square. Legal-move filtering is trial-and-revert: tentatively apply the candidate, ask if your own king is attacked, revert. Checkmate is then brutally simple: the side to move is in check and `hasAnyLegalMove` returns false. Stalemate is the same with no check. **Why trial-and-revert instead of simulation on a copied board?** Copying the board per candidate is O(64) allocation per trial and invites aliasing bugs when pieces are mutable. Trial-and-revert mutates two references and restores them — faster to write correctly, but you must remember the en passant victim square as a third mutation. State that handling explicitly; interviewers probe it. Performance note: `hasAnyLegalMove` is the only expensive call and it runs once per move — acceptable for interactive play, unacceptable for a search engine, which is why real engines use incremental attack tables. Name that boundary: your design is correct for a game server, not for Stockfish.

blocks.title: The pinned-piece trap
blocks.text: A move can be geometrically perfect and still illegal because it **exposes your own king**. Every move — not just king moves — must pass the *leaves-king-in-check* filter, including en passant captures that open a diagonal. Candidates who only validate the king's destination fail pinned-rook cases. If you remember one line, remember this: **legality = geometry + king safety, always.**

blocks.title: Game lifecycle
blocks.caption: Status is derived after every commit, never stored incrementally.
blocks.code:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> IN_PROGRESS
  IN_PROGRESS --> IN_PROGRESS : legal move no mate
  IN_PROGRESS --> WHITE_WINS : black mated
  IN_PROGRESS --> BLACK_WINS : white mated
  IN_PROGRESS --> STALEMATE : no legal move no check
  WHITE_WINS --> [*]
  BLACK_WINS --> [*]
  STALEMATE --> [*]

blocks.text: Follow-ups to have ready

items.title: Undo / redo
items.text: You already keep enough: store inverse deltas (moved piece, captured piece, prev hasMoved flags, prev lastMove) on a stack. Do not re-derive by replaying history — O(n) replay is a trap. Pop and restore in O(1).

items.title: Timed play and draws
items.text: Add a Clock interface injected into Game, plus fifty-move counter and position-hash map for threefold repetition. Keep them outside Board — time is not board state.

items.title: Pawn promotion choice
items.text: Change commitMove to accept a PieceType parameter defaulting to queen. Underpromotion to knight matters for stalemate avoidance — mention it to signal you know the rule exists.

items.title: Multiplayer / persistence
items.text: Make Board serialisable to FEN strings and Move to long algebraic notation. Game becomes a thin session over an event log — the same trial-and-revert core serves networked play unchanged.

items.title: Engine hook
items.text: Expose getLegalMoves(color) returning a list built on hasAnyLegalMove primitives. Search lives above the rules engine and never touches validation internals. That separation is the Strategy pattern answer if asked.

blocks.text: Edge cases to state unprompted

items: Moving when it is not your turn, moving an empty square, or capturing your own piece — reject before geometry.
Sliding through or onto a friendly piece; knight jumping is the only exception to blocking.
Pawn moving backward, capturing straight, or double-stepping from a non-start rank or over an occupied square.
En passant only on the immediately following move after an adjacent pawn's double-step — expires otherwise.
Castling through check, out of check, with a moved king or rook, or with pieces between — all illegal.
Promotion on the last rank must replace the pawn before status evaluation; a fresh queen can deliver mate.
Any move — including a discovered pin — that leaves your own king in check is illegal, even if the piece move is valid.
Stalemate vs checkmate: no legal moves with no check is a draw, not a win — compute both conditions.

blocks.text: What you are graded on

blocks.caption: Weak vs strong signals for this problem.
rows: One class with switch on piece type
Geometry in pieces, legality and king-safety in game, grid in board
Turn + ownership + geometry + path + own-king-safety in fixed order
Forgot or hand-waved castling / en passant
Rights flags + lastMove + attacked-square rule stated precisely
Attacked-square primitive reused for check, mate, stalemate, castling
New rule edits one giant method
New piece = new subclass; undo = move stack; patterns named
States trade-offs: grid vs bitboard, trial vs copy, clarity vs engine speed

blocks.title: Your 45-minute plan
blocks.text: Minutes 0-8: clarify scope and lock the API. 8-15: sketch the three-layer diagram and defend the split. 15-32: code `Piece`, two sliders, `Board.isPathClear`, and `Game.makeMove` with the king-safety filter — narrate each gate. 32-40: add en passant, castling, promotion, then `isInCheck` and `hasAnyLegalMove`. 40-45: walk a pinned-rook case and a castling-through-check case out loud, then name undo and repetition as ready follow-ups.
